## buildkite
This is the Buildkite MCP Server. It provides access to the Buildkite CI/CD API, enabling you to manage and inspect pipelines, builds, jobs, logs, clusters, tests, artifacts, and annotations.

Start here: Before using most tools, call user_token_organization to retrieve the organization slug. Nearly every other tool requires the org_slug parameter, and this call is the fastest way to discover it.

Skill discovery: Always call list_skills early in a session — it's cheap (names and one-line descriptions only) and surfaces guidance not visible in any tool's name or schema. When a task matches a listed skill (e.g. debugging a build failure, tuning search_logs), call load_skill for that guide — it covers parameter tuning, caching behavior, and details beyond the summaries below.

Authorization: Tools available depend on the scopes granted to the configured API token. A 401 response from a tool means the token lacks the required scope for that operation.

Common pitfalls:

build_number is a sequential integer string (e.g. "42"), not a UUID. Build, job, artifact, and log tools all require this identifier — do not use the build's UUID id field.

Job state "broken" means the job did not run because something inside the build prevented execution: an if conditional evaluated to false, a branch filter did not match, or an upstream dependency failed. It does not mean the job's command failed. Distinguish: broken = build configuration or dependencies prevented execution; failed = job ran but exited non-zero; skipped = external factor (e.g. a newer build superseded it). When both failed and broken jobs are present, investigate failed upstream jobs first.

Log investigation order: start with tail_logs to see recent output (cheapest, catches most failures), then search_logs with a pattern and limit for targeted investigation, and only use read_logs with seek and limit for deep sequential inspection. Avoid calling read_logs without a limit on large logs.

## claude.ai Honeycomb
Honeycomb MCP Server - Observability Data Query Interface

<role>
You are an observability assistant for Honeycomb users. You investigate production behavior — performance, errors, deployment impact, alert state — by querying real telemetry through these tools. The workspace's actual state is only knowable through tool calls; do not reason from priors about what services, datasets, or alerts exist.

When the user names a dataset, span, or service, treat it as a starting point for discovery, not a license to skip it. The right span name within a dataset is rarely obvious from the dataset name alone, and aggregating the wrong attribute or the wrong span is the most common cause of misleading answers.
</role>

<workflow>
For most observability questions — including "how many", "what's slow", "what's erroring" — start with span discovery (list_spans, get_span_details). These tools return counts and attribute distributions directly; they often answer the question without a follow-up query. Reach for run_query only when you need a calculation, distribution, or comparison those tools can't express. Span tools work across all trace-aware datasets in scope without needing to know which dataset to target.

1. ORIENT
   - Call 'get_workspace_context' to learn the team, environments, and dataset counts. Use the returned environment slug in subsequent calls.

2. DISCOVER (pick the path that matches the question)
   - Span discovery — for "what's happening / what's slow / how many X / what does service X do":
     - 'list_spans' ranks span names by count with root_count to distinguish entry points from internal helpers. Counts here are often the answer to "how many X happened".
     - 'get_span_details' on a chosen span_name returns its populated attributes, value cardinality, and top observed values — including which spans actually populate a count-bearing attribute.
     Answer directly from these when you can — composing an equivalent run_query by hand is slower and more error-prone.

## plugin:datadog:mcp
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). Consult Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. - address-findings: Address the review findings posted on an Entire trail: fetch the trail's open findings, fix the code, and resolve them on the trail. Use when the user gives a trail URL or number and asks to address, fix, or resolve its findings or review comments. Not for local diff review — that is the `review` skill.
- after-hours: Unattended autonomous work mode for explicit after-hours, overnight, while-away, prototype, spike, or plan-execution requests where the user wants Codex to keep working without step-by-step approval and leave a handoff report.
- clean-go: Focused Go clean-code review and fix workflow for the current diff against origin/main, based on modern Go and local Go preferences. By default, fixes only high-confidence, unambiguous Required findings in one batch. Use when the user asks for clean Go review, Go cleanliness, Go refactoring review, pfleidi:clean-go, or when larger Go refactors/code changes need clean Go guidance.
- daily-handoff: Summarize a day's activity as a handoff: a short bulleted list of what the user did plus 5 concrete next steps, pulled from Slack (including personal "what's next" notes-to-self), the user's active Claude Code sessions, and GitHub PRs created or merged that day. Also surfaces ready-to-run commands to resume every Claude session from that day in case the machine is restarted, and feeds a desktop buddy. Defaults to today; accepts an optional day override (a weekday name, today, yesterday, or YYYY-MM-DD). Use when the user says "daily handoff", "handoff", "wrap up my day", "weekend handoff", or "/daily-handoff".
- incident: incident.io assistant for working with incidents. View incident details, post updates to incident channels, interact with the incident agent, and query structured incident data. Use whenever the user mentions an incident ID (e.g., "INC-123"), asks about an incident, or uses the /incident command. Trigger proactively when you see an incident reference.
- pr: Create a pull request for the current branch. Discovers and deduplicates the project's build/lint/test setup from Makefile, mise, CI config, or README and runs verification before pushing. Automatically fixes any verification failures and prompts the user to commit before proceeding. Opens a draft PR by default unless the user explicitly asks for a ready-for-review PR. Accepts an optional PR target base branch (defaults to main); scope checks always compare branch-only changes from the merge base with origin/main. Use when the user says "create pr", "open pr", "make pr", or "/pr".
- pr-feedback: Fetch PR review comments, separate human from bot feedback, and address them differently. Bot comments and high-confidence unambiguous human comments are fixed in one pass. Ambiguous human comments are left unresolved with the exact decision needed. Publishes addressed/rejected threads while leaving Needs decision threads untouched. Accepts an optional PR number or URL; defaults to the PR for the current branch. Use when the user says "fix pr comments", "address pr feedback", "pr feedback", or "/pr-feedback".
- review: Parallel multi-lens code review against origin/main. Spawns security, correctness, simplification, readability, and conditional Go clean-code/modern-Go agents, runs an independent second-pass coverage sweep, verifies findings against source, and presents a deduplicated severity-ranked report. By default, fixes only high-confidence, unambiguous Required findings in one batch. No commits are made — code changes only, user commits on their own terms. Use when the user says "review", "review this branch", "code review", "full review", or "/review".
- testing: Local testing strategy and review guidance for meaningful tests, choosing unit vs integration vs end-to-end scope, avoiding production-only test seams and over-mocking, and keeping test helpers readable, especially in Go. Use when writing, changing, or reviewing tests; adding mocks or test helpers; deciding test scope; or when user mentions pfleidi:testing.
- writing-ruleset: Use when drafting or revising prose for a human reader — chat replies, emails, documents, specs, articles, UI text, reviews, or criticism — especially to fit the medium, audience, and task and avoid generic chatbot defaults.
- agent-integration: Run all three agent integration phases sequentially: research, write-tests, and implement using E2E-first TDD (unit tests written last). Use when the user says "integrate agent", "add agent support", or wants to run the full agent integration pipeline end-to-end.
- changelog: Generate or update the CHANGELOG.md for a new release version. Use when the user says "generate changelog", "update changelog", "write release notes", or asks to prepare a changelog for a version like "changelog for 0.5.3".
- e2e: Orchestrate E2E test triage and fix implementation: runs triage-ci then implement sequentially. Accepts test names, --agent, artifact path, or CI run reference. - explain: Explains the intent behind source code by finding original session transcripts. Use explain with a function, file, or line of code to understand why it exists.
- search: Use when the user wants to find prior work, checkpoints, or agent conversations by topic, repo, branch, author, or recent time window

Base directory for this skill: /Users/ninawork/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.2.0/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];

    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**The terminal state is invoking writing-plans.** Do NOT invoke frontend-design, mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. The ONLY skill you invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT offer it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, offer it then, as its own message:
> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

content.text:
Here's how it works today, and where the constraint actually is.

## How trail listing works now

`entire trail list` is **repo-scoped**. It resolves a `forge/owner/repo` triple and hits a per-repo endpoint:

- Resolution: `resolveTrailRepoOrRemote` → either the `--repo` flag or the `origin` remote of the current clone (`trail_cmd.go:451`, `2004`).
- Endpoint: `GET /api/v1/trails/{forge}/{owner}/{repo}` (`trailsBasePath`, `trail_cmd.go:1974`).

So "not in a repo" fails simply because there's no origin remote to resolve, and no default repo triple.

**There's already a partial escape hatch:** the persistent `--repo` flag (`trail_cmd.go:77`) lets you list/show a repo you're *not* checked out in — `entire trail list --repo gh/entireio/cli` works from anywhere. It's just per-repo and you have to name the repo.

## The two directions you raised — and their real cost

**1. "List trails for repos enabled locally."** The blocker: there is **no machine-level registry of enabled repos**. Enablement is stored per-clone in each repo's git common dir (`ClonePreferences`, `settings.go:164`; the trails-enablement cache is keyed to a single clone's origin, `trail_context_cache.go:44-72`). So to do this today we'd have to either scan the filesystem for clones or build a new "enrolled clones" registry — and it still only covers repos you happen to have cloned, not everything you have access to.

**2. "List all trails the user has access to for their account."** This is the cleaner fit. There's an established **account-scoped `/me/*` family** on the entire-api cell that already aggregates across repos in your home cell — `/me/activity`, `/me/sessions`, `/me/commits`, `/me/recap` (`activity_cmd.go:140-182`). A `/me/trails` endpoint would slot right into that pattern, and the CLI side (`entire trail list` with no repo → account-wide) becomes straightforward. The cost: it needs a **server endpoint that doesn't exist yet** (entire-api, not this repo).

My recommendation is **option 2** — it's the complete solution, matches existing precedent, and option 1's local-registry work buys you a strictly smaller answer.

Before I go further into design, one thing determines the whole shape of this:

content.content:
1	package cli
2	
3	import (
4		"context"
5		"errors"
6		"io"
7		"strings"
8		"time"
9	
10		"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/api"
11		"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/auth"
12		"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/gitremote"
13		"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/logging"
14		"github.com/entireio/cli/internal/coreapi"
15	)
16	
17	// currentRepoRefTimeout bounds currentRepoRef's control-plane lookup. The
18	// lookup is best-effort decoration (recap degrades to personal-only without
19	// it), so a stalled core must not hang the command — mirror cellResolveTimeout.
20	const currentRepoRefTimeout = 5 * time.Second
21	
22	// runAuthenticatedActivityAPI runs fn with an authenticated client for the
23	// activity/recap surface. It prefers the caller's home entire-api cell (the same
24	// shared client the experts commands use), which serves the /me/* endpoints
25	// these commands call.
26	//
27	// Cell routing is a best-effort upgrade: any failure building the cell client —
28	// the region has no cell yet (ErrNoCellForJurisdiction), not logged in, or a
29	// discovery/exchange error — falls back to the data API, which also serves
30	// /me/* and yields the canonical auth errors (e.g. the "not logged in" hint).
31	// This keeps the migration transparent and non-regressive; non-obvious
32	// fallbacks are logged for diagnosis. Both backends expose the same /me/* paths,
33	// so fn is agnostic to which client it receives.
34	func runAuthenticatedActivityAPI(ctx context.Context, errW io.Writer, insecureHTTP bool, fn func(context.Context, *api.Client) error) error {
35		client, err := auth.NewEntireAPICellClient(ctx, insecureHTTP, nil)
36		if err != nil {
37			logCellClientFallback(ctx, err)
38			return runAuthenticatedDataAPI(ctx, errW, insecureHTTP, fn)
39		}
40		return fn(ctx, client)
41	}
42	
43	// logCellClientFallback records, at debug, that an activity/recap command fell
44	// back from the entire-api cell to the data API. The expected cases — the
45	// region has no cell yet, or the caller isn't logged in — aren't logged: they
46	// are normal during rollout and on first use, not diagnosable failures.
47	func logCellClientFallback(ctx context.Context, err error) {
48		if errors.Is(err, auth.ErrNoCellForJurisdiction) || errors.Is(err, auth.ErrNotLoggedIn) {
49			return
50		}
51		logging.Debug(ctx, "activity/recap: entire-api cell client unavailable, using data API", "error", err.Error())
52	}
53	
54	// forgeToMirrorProvider maps a gitremote forge identifier (e.g. "gh") to the
55	// upstream provider the control plane records mirrors under (e.g. "github").
56	// entire-api routing only supports GitHub mirrors today.
57	func forgeToMirrorProvider(forge string) (string, bool) {
58		switch strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(forge)) {
59		case "gh", mirrorCloneProviderGitHub:
60			return mirrorCloneProviderGitHub, true
61		default:
62			return "", false
63		}
64	}
65	
66	// currentRepoRef best-effort resolves the current repo (its "origin" remote)
67	// to the ULID entire-api uses for repo-scoped params — recap's /me/recap?repo=
68	// — plus the human owner/repo slug for display, from a single remote
69	// resolution (the caller needs both; resolving twice would double the git and
70	// control-plane work). entire.io/api documents the mirror id as exactly that
71	// repo_id (repo_id = mirror_repos.id), and the CLI already lists mirrors via
72	// the control plane, so no extra resolution is needed. Any failure returns
73	// "", "" — recap then shows the personal side only rather than erroring.
74	func currentRepoRef(ctx context.Context) (repoID, repoSlug string) {
75		ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, currentRepoRefTimeout)
76		defer cancel()
77	
78		forge, owner, repo, err := gitremote.ResolveRemoteRepo(ctx, "origin")
79		if err != nil || owner == "" || repo == "" {
80			return "", ""
81		}
82		provider, ok := forgeToMirrorProvider(forge)
83		if !ok {
84			return "", ""
85		}
86		c, err := coreapi.New()
87		if err != nil {
88			return "", ""
89		}
90		mirrors, err := listMirrorsForRepo(ctx, c, provider, strings.ToLower(owner), repo)
91		if err != nil {
92			return "", ""
93		}
94		repoID = firstActiveRepoID(mirrors)
95		if repoID == "" {
96			return "", ""
97		}
98		return repoID, owner + "/" + repo
99	}
100	
101	// firstActiveRepoID returns the id of the repo's first active mirror (the repo
102	// id is stable across a repo's placements, so any active one serves). Archived
103	// and failed/suspended placements are skipped — they can't answer for the repo.
104	func firstActiveRepoID(mirrors []coreapi.Mirror) string {
105		for i := range mirrors {
106			if !isActiveMirror(mirrors[i]) {
107				continue
108			}
109			if id := strings.TrimSpace(mirrors[i].MirrorId); id != "" {
110				return id
111			}
112		}
113		return ""
114	}

content.text:
I've got the CLI side mapped. Account-wide listing will route through the **home-cell client** (`runAuthenticatedActivityAPI` → `auth.NewEntireAPICellClient`, with data-API fallback), exactly like `/me/activity` — not the repo-scoped data-API client that today's `entire trail list` uses. So the CLI design is:

- `--repo X` → repo-scoped (unchanged)
- `--all`, or no resolvable origin → account-wide `GET /api/v1/me/trails` via the cell client
- otherwise → repo-scoped via origin (unchanged); the current hard error on "no origin" becomes the auto-fallback trigger

I've dispatched two parallel explorations of `entire-api` for the parts I can't design without: the **trails data source + access-control rule** (what "has access to this repo's trails" means in code, so the account query applies the same rule) and the **`/me/*` handler pattern** (routing, home-cell aggregation, where a new handler slots in). I'll fold their findings into the design doc once they report back.

- **`/me/*`**: `requireAuth(api, &userDeps.baseDeps)` only (`me.go:29`, `me_sessions.go:77`). content.text:
Both explorations are in. Track B surfaced the key architectural correction, so let me present the design before writing it up.

## Design: repo-less trail listing via account-scoped `/me/trails`

### 1. Server shape — it's a `/cache/prs`, not a `/me/activity`
This is the important finding. Trails do **not** live in the per-user `my_activity` spine — they live in the repo store (`repo_trails`, keyed by `repo_id`, each row carrying `author_account_id`). So `/me/trails` follows the **`internal/httpapi/cache_prs.go`** pattern, not `/me/activity`:

1. `requireAuth` only, no per-repo gate.
2. Enumerate the caller's repos with `memberRepoSet(ctx, deps.Reader)` — SpiceDB `repo/list` (direct grants + project membership, excludes the `public_viewer` wildcard). This matches `/repos` and `/cache/prs`; "trails across my repos" shouldn't pull in every public repo.
3. New repo-store method `TrailsForRepos(ctx, repoIDs, filters)` in `internal/store/trails.go`, alongside `ListTrailsByRepo` — `SELECT ... FROM repo_trails WHERE repo_id = ANY($1) [AND status filters] [AND author_account_id = caller] ORDER BY updated_at DESC LIMIT $n`.
4. Label each row with `repo_full_name` + `is_private` via the existing `repoDisplay`/`repoMetaMap` helpers.

New file `internal/httpapi/me_trails.go` (`registerMeTrails(api, deps *RepoActivityDeps)`), registered in `router.go`'s `NewActivityAPIRouter` next to `registerMe`. Reuses `requireAuth`, `id(ctx)`, `memberRepoSet`, `teamOp`, `repoDisplay`, `isoTime`.

### 2. ⚠️ Contract drift I need your call on
The local **entire-api** `repo_trails` list route serves `pageSize`/`pageToken` → `{items, nextPageToken}` with **no status/author/limit filtering**. The local **CLI** sends `status/author/limit/offset` → `{trails, total}`. The two local checkouts disagree on the repo-scoped contract (entire-api `main` was refactored to keyset pagination — commit history shows recent ENT-1231 work).

For the **new** `/me/trails` I control the contract. My proposal:
- Params: `status` (optional, comma-list), `author=me` (optional → `author_account_id = caller`; no gh-CLI login lookup needed for the account-wide path), `limit` (clamped, default 200).
- Response: `{items: [...], total}` — each item = existing `TrailListItem` + `repoFullName` + `isPrivate`.
- No keyset cursor in v1 (limit-capped, matching the `/me/sessions` limit convention).

This means account-wide and repo-scoped paths won't share an identical wire contract, but the CLI's *account-wide* code is new so it just targets this shape.

### 3. CLI wiring (this repo)

input.content:
# Account-scoped trail listing (`/me/trails`)

Date: 2026-07-28
Repos touched: `entire-api` (new endpoint), `cli` (wiring)

## Problem

`entire trail list` (and the other trail commands) only work from inside a
checked-out repo with a supported `origin` remote. `resolveTrailRepoOrRemote`
resolves a single `forge/owner/repo` triple from `origin` (or the `--repo`
flag) and calls the per-repo endpoint `GET /api/v1/trails/{host}/{owner}/{repo}`
(`cli` `trail_cmd.go:451`, `1974`). With no origin there is no default triple,
so the command errors.

Requiring a checked-out repo just to *list* trails is friction: a user should
be able to see the trails they have access to across all their repos from
anywhere.

## Goals

- `entire trail list` works with no repo checked out, listing trails across all
  repos the caller is a member of.
- Optionally narrow that account-wide list to a subset of repos.
- Reuse the established account-scoped (`/me/*`) and cross-repo (`/cache/prs`)
  server patterns and the home-cell client on the CLI side.

## Non-goals

- Creating a trail from outside a repo (branch+repo bound; tracked separately).
- Cross-jurisdiction aggregation. `/me/trails` is home-cell-only, matching all
  other `/me/*` endpoints; client-side federation is a later follow-up.
- Reconciling the pre-existing repo-scoped list contract drift (tracked in a
  separate local handoff note, not in this spec).

## Server: `/me/trails` endpoint (entire-api)

### Architecture — a `/cache/prs`, not a `/me/activity`

Trails are **repo-store** data (`repo_trails`, keyed by `repo_id`, each row
carrying `author_account_id`) — they are *not* in the per-user `my_activity`
spine. So the endpoint is shaped like `internal/httpapi/cache_prs.go`
(`registerCachePRs`), a cross-repo "your X across your repos" read that needs
only `repoDeps`:

1. `requireAuth` only, no per-repo gate (`router.go:471`).
2. Resolve caller: `id(ctx)` → `auth.FromContext(ctx).AccountID`
   (`experimental_me.go:257`).
3. Enumerate the caller's repos with `memberRepoSet(ctx, deps.Reader)` —
   SpiceDB `repo/list`: direct grants + project membership, **excludes** the
   `public_viewer` wildcard (`perreq.go:53`). Same set `/repos` and
   `/cache/prs` use.
4. If a `repo` filter is present, resolve each `forge/owner/repo` →
   `repo_id` via `RepoIDByFullName` (`store/repo_aggregates.go:559`) and
   **intersect** with the member set. The filter can only narrow, never widen,
   what the caller may see.
5. Query the repo store with the resolved id set (new method, below).
6. Label each row with `repo_full_name` + `is_private` via `repoDisplay` /
   `repoMetaMap` (`me.go:551`, `457`).

### Access model

Default set = **membership** (`repo/list`). Chosen over the accessible/pull set
so the personal list does not pull in every public repo the caller can read.
The `repo` filter still intersects with this set, so access is always
authoritative.

### Wire contract (defined fresh for this endpoint)

Request `GET /api/v1/me/trails`:

| param    | type            | notes                                                             |
|----------|-----------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `status` | comma-list enum | optional; omitted = all statuses                                  |
| `author` | string          | optional; `me` → `author_account_id = caller`. (Arbitrary login not supported in v1 — account-wide has no gh-CLI login lookup.) |
| `repo`   | repeatable / comma-list | optional; each `forge/owner/repo`, intersected with member set |
| `limit`  | int             | clamped (default 200, max TBD in plan)                            |

Response body:

```jsonc
{
  "items": [
    { /* existing TrailListItem fields */
      "repoFullName": "acme/app",
      "isPrivate": true
    }
  ],
  "total": 42
}
```

`items[]` = the existing `TrailListItem` (`trails_types.go:25`) plus
`repoFullName` and `isPrivate`. `total` = full match count for the filters.
No keyset cursor in v1 (limit-capped, matching the `/me/sessions` limit
convention). Sort `updated_at DESC, id DESC`.

### Implementation shape

- **New file** `internal/httpapi/me_trails.go`: `func registerMeTrails(api
  huma.API, deps *RepoActivityDeps)`; input/output structs
  (`MeTrailsInput` / `MeTrailsOutput`), or add the types alongside
  `MeSessionsOutput` in `me_types.go`. Register under the `me` Huma tag.
- **Register** in `internal/httpapi/router.go` `NewActivityAPIRouter`, next to
  `registerMe(...)` / `registerMeSessions(...)` (`router.go:414`).
- **New store method** in `internal/store/trails.go`, alongside
  `ListTrailsByRepo` (`trails.go:67`):
  `TrailsForRepos(ctx, repoIDs [][]byte, filters) ([]TrailListRow, error)` —
  `SELECT ... FROM repo_trails WHERE repo_id = ANY($1) [AND status = ANY(...)]
  [AND author_account_id = $caller] ORDER BY updated_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT $n`,
  plus a count for `total`.
- **Reuse, do not re-implement**: `requireAuth`, `id(ctx)`, `memberRepoSet`,
  `teamOp` (`repos.go:26`), `repoDisplay`/`repoMetaMap`, `isoTime`,
  `resolveAuthorLogins` (`trails.go:265`) for author id→login display.

## CLI wiring (cli)

### Routing rule for `entire trail list`

- **exactly one repo** (`--repo X`, or resolvable `origin`, and no `--all`) →
  repo-scoped endpoint, unchanged. Kept deliberately: the repo-scoped path hits
  the repo's *own* cell, so it is cross-cell safe.
- **zero repos** (no origin / not in a repo), or `--all`, or **multiple repos**
  → account-wide `GET /api/v1/me/trails`, with any repo values passed as the
  `repo` filter.
- Today's hard error on "no resolvable origin" becomes the auto-fallback
  trigger into the account-wide path.

### Client

Account-wide requests use `runAuthenticatedActivityAPI`
(`entireapi_client.go:34`) — the home-cell `auth.NewEntireAPICellClient` with a
data-API fallback — **not** the repo-scoped `runAuthenticatedTrailAPI`
(`trail_context_cache.go:480`) that today's list uses. This is the same client
`/me/activity` and `/me/sessions` use.

### Flags & display

- `--all` (new): force account-wide even inside a repo.
- `--repo`: single value keeps repo-scoped routing (unchanged). Multiple values
  (comma-list or repeatable) route account-wide as a filter. Flag mechanics —
  `--repo` is currently a single persistent `StringVar` on the whole `trail`
  tree (`trail_cmd.go:77`) used by `show`/`checkout` as a single target; the
  plan must pick between accepting a comma-list on the existing flag (with
  single-value validation kept for the subcommands that need exactly one) vs. a
  dedicated list flag scoped to `list`.
- `--status`, `--author me`, `--limit`, `--json` all still apply to the
  account-wide path.
- Account-wide human output adds a **repo column** to `printTrailList`
  (`trail_cmd.go:622`); repo-scoped output is unchanged.

## Limitation

Home-cell only: `/me/trails` sees trails for repos placed in the caller's home
cell that they are a member of. No server-side cross-cell fan-out — consistent
with every `/me/*` endpoint. A `repo` filter naming a repo hosted in another
cell returns nothing from `/me/trails`; that single repo is better listed via
the repo-scoped path (which is why single `--repo` stays repo-scoped).

## Testing

- **entire-api**: store-level test for `TrailsForRepos` (id-set filter, status
  filter, author filter, ordering, limit/total). httpapi test for
  `/me/trails`: membership gating (a non-member repo's trails never appear),
  the `repo` filter intersecting with membership (cannot widen access), and
  the response shape incl. `repoFullName`/`isPrivate`. Follow the
  `cache_prs` / `me_sessions` test patterns.
- **cli**: routing tests — one repo vs. zero vs. multiple vs. `--all` picks the
  right endpoint/client; account-wide `--json` output; repo column rendering;
  `--author me` maps to the account filter. Use `execx.NonInteractive` for any
  real-binary spawns.

## Sequencing

1. entire-api: `TrailsForRepos` store method + `/me/trails` handler + tests.
2. cli: routing + flags + display + tests, targeting the new contract.

The CLI account-wide path depends on the entire-api endpoint existing, so land
the server side first (or behind the same review).

# Handoff: repo-scoped trail-list contract drift (CLI ↔ entire-api)

Not part of the `/me/trails` work — flagged and deferred during that design.
This file is intentionally **uncommitted**. Delete it once triaged.

## What

The repo-scoped trail-list endpoint has two different contracts between the
local checkouts:

**CLI** (`cli`) sends and expects:
- Request params: `status`, `author`, `limit`, `offset`
  (`cmd/entire/cli/trail_cmd.go:524` `trailListQueryWithOffset`)
- Response: `{ "trails": [...], "total": N }`
  (`cmd/entire/cli/api/trail_types.go:12` `TrailListResponse`)

**entire-api** (`internal/httpapi/trails.go`, `main`) serves:
- Request params: `pageSize` (1–100, default 50), `pageToken` (opaque keyset
  cursor) — **no** `status` / `author` / `limit` / `offset`, no server-side
  filtering
- Response: `{ "items": [...], "nextPageToken": ... }` — **no** `total`
  (`internal/httpapi/trails_types.go:51` `TrailsListResponse`)

So the CLI's `--status` / `--author` / `--limit` filters and its `total`-based
"N of M" summary rely on a contract the local entire-api `main` does not
implement. The CLI has a defensive fallback ("older servers don't report a
total; fall back to page size", `trail_cmd.go:482`), which suggests the
contracts diverged over time.

## Why it matters

- Filters may be silently ignored server-side (client filters nothing; server
  returns everything up to a page).
- Truncation/summary counts may be wrong.
- Unclear which contract production actually serves — the shipped CLI talks to
  production, so production likely still honors the filter contract, meaning
  entire-api `main` may be mid-refactor (keyset) and ahead of / behind the CLI.

## Next step (triage)

1. Confirm what **production** entire-api serves for
   `GET /api/v1/trails/{host}/{owner}/{repo}` (filter contract vs. keyset).
2. Decide the single source of truth and align the other side.
3. If keyset is the target, update the CLI list client + `TrailListResponse`
   and re-express `--status`/`--author`/`--limit` (server-side filters or
   client-side over the cursor).

## Suggested issue / trail template

> **Title:** Repo-scoped trail list contract drift: CLI filters/`total` vs
> entire-api keyset pagination
>
> **Body:** The CLI's `entire trail list` sends `status`/`author`/`limit`/
> `offset` and reads `{trails,total}`, but entire-api `main` serves
> `pageSize`/`pageToken` → `{items,nextPageToken}` with no server-side
> filtering. Confirm the production contract, pick one source of truth, and
> align both sides. Surfaced while designing account-scoped `/me/trails`
> (see `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-28-account-scoped-trail-listing-design.md`).

  (`cmd/entire/cli/trail_cmd.go:524` `trailListQueryWithOffset`)
- Response: `{ "trails": [...], "total": N }`
  (`cmd/entire/cli/api/trail_types.go:12` `TrailListResponse`)

**entire-api** (`internal/httpapi/trails.go`, `main`) serves:
- Request params: `pageSize` (1–100, default 50), `pageToken` (opaque keyset
  cursor) — **no** `status` / `author` / `limit` / `offset`, no server-side
  filtering
- Response: `{ "items": [...], "nextPageToken": ... }` — **no** `total`
  (`internal/httpapi/trails_types.go:51` `TrailsListResponse`)

So the CLI's `--status` / `--author` / `--limit` filters and its `total`-based
"N of M" summary rely on a contract the local entire-api `main` does not
implement. The CLI has a defensive fallback ("older servers don't report a
total; fall back to page size", `trail_cmd.go:482`), which suggests the
contracts diverged over time.

## Why it matters

- Filters may be silently ignored server-side (client filters nothing; server
  returns everything up to a page).
- Truncation/summary counts may be wrong.
- Unclear which contract production actually serves — the shipped CLI talks to
  production, so production likely still honors the filter contract, meaning
  entire-api `main` may be mid-refactor (keyset) and ahead of / behind the CLI.

## Next step (triage)

1. Confirm what **production** entire-api serves for
   `GET /api/v1/trails/{host}/{owner}/{repo}` (filter contract vs. keyset).
2. Decide the single source of truth and align the other side.
3. If keyset is the target, update the CLI list client + `TrailListResponse`
   and re-express `--status`/`--author`/`--limit` (server-side filters or
   client-side over the cursor).

## Suggested issue / trail template

> **Title:** Repo-scoped trail list contract drift: CLI filters/`total` vs
> entire-api keyset pagination
>
> **Body:** The CLI's `entire trail list` sends `status`/`author`/`limit`/
> `offset` and reads `{trails,total}`, but entire-api `main` serves
> `pageSize`/`pageToken` → `{items,nextPageToken}` with no server-side
> filtering. Confirm the production contract, pick one source of truth, and
> align both sides. Surfaced while designing account-scoped `/me/trails`
> (see `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-28-account-scoped-trail-listing-design.md`).

# i-have-adhd

The reader has ADHD. Output is not just brief. It is shaped so an ADHD brain can act on it.

## Persistence

These rules apply to every response for the rest of the session, not only this one. They do not expire after a few turns and they do not lapse when the topic changes. If you are unsure whether they still apply, they do.

Turn them off only when the reader says "stop adhd mode" or "normal mode". Confirm in one line, then return to your default style.

## What ADHD changes about reading

Four facts drive every rule below:

1. Working memory is small. Anything not on screen is forgotten. Do not ask the reader to "keep in mind X."
2. Knowing the answer is not doing the answer. The friction between "got it" and "done it" is where work dies.
3. Starting is the hardest step. The first action must be obvious, small, and doable now.
4. Dopamine is scarce. Visible progress matters. Buried wins do not register.

## Rules

### 1. Lead with the next action

The first line is something the reader can do. Not context. Not a plan. The action.

Bad: "Let's think about this. Your auth flow has a few moving pieces..."
Good: "Run `npm install jsonwebtoken`, then edit `src/auth.ts:42`."

If the answer is a command, path, or snippet, it goes first. Prose comes after, if at all.

### 2. Number multi-step tasks

If the work takes more than one step, write a numbered list. Each step is one bounded action. No step contains "and then" twice.

Use the fewest steps that still work. Cut any step the reader does not need, and fold trivial steps into the one before. A short path finished beats a complete path abandoned.

Bad: "First open the file, find the function, swap it out, then run the tests."

Good:
```
1. Open `src/auth.ts`
2. Replace `verifyToken` (lines 42 to 58) with the snippet below
3. Run `npm test -- auth.spec.ts`
```

### 3. End with one concrete next action

If anything is left open, name ONE thing the reader can do in under two minutes. Even "open the file" counts.

Bad: "Hope that helps. Let me know if you want to dig deeper."
Good: "Next: run `npm test` and paste the first failing line."

### 4. Suppress tangents

If a second issue exists, finish the first, then offer the second as a separate question.

Bad: "Here's the fix. By the way, your dependency is also stale, and your README is out of date, and..."
Good: "Here's the fix. Separately: there is also a stale dependency. Want me to handle that next?"

A question that comes up mid-work is not a tangent: answer it yourself if you can and fold the result in. If it still needs the reader, surface it once, at the end.

### 5. Restate state every turn

The reader cannot hold "we are on step 3 of 5" between messages. Restate it.

Bad: "Done. Ready for the next part?"
Good: "Step 3 of 5 done: schema updated. Next: backfill the new column. Run the script?"

If the harness has a task or plan tool, use it for multi-step work: one item per step, one in progress at a time. The checklist does the restating; do not also narrate the full plan as prose.

### 6. Make completed work visible

Show what now works, in concrete terms. Do not bury wins in a recap.

Bad: "I've made some changes to the auth flow. Among other things..."
Good: "Login now works with magic links. Try: `npm run dev`, open `/login`."

### 7. Matter-of-fact tone for errors

Never use "Uh oh," "Oh no," or "There seems to be a problem." State cause and fix.

Bad: "Uh oh, the test is failing. There seems to be an issue..."
Good: "Test fails at `auth.spec.ts:42`: expected 200, got 401. Cause: missing auth header. Fix: add `Authorization: Bearer ${token}` to the request."

### 8. Cap lists at 5 items

If a list grows past five, split into "do now" vs "later," or "must" vs "nice to have." Five items ranked beats ten unranked.

### 9. No preamble, no recap, no closing pleasantries

Forbidden openers: "Great question," "Let me...", "I'll...", "Sure!", "Looking at your...", "To answer your question..."

Forbidden recaps after a completed task: "I've now done X, Y, and Z, which means..."

Forbidden closers: "Let me know if you need anything else," "Hope this helps," "Happy to clarify," "Feel free to ask."

Start with the answer. End when the answer is done.

## When to break the rules

Override the defaults when:

1. User asks to "explain" or "walk me through." Explain fully. Still no preamble, still no closer, but the body runs as long as the topic needs. Add headers so the reader can skim back.
2. Destructive action ahead (`rm -rf`, force push, schema migration, dropping a table). Confirm before acting. Safety wins over brevity.
3. Debug spiral. If the last three turns have been "still broken," stop iterating on code. Name the assumption that might be wrong. Ask one diagnostic question.
4. Real ambiguity in the request. One short clarifying question beats guessing and rewriting.
5. A rule fights the task. When a rule would delete the answer itself, the task wins; the shape stays. Example: "what are my options" gets 2 to 4 ranked options with one-line trade-offs, recommendation first, not one path. The options are the answer.
6. A rule fights the harness. Inside an agent harness, the system prompt outranks this skill: announce a tool call when the harness requires it, do the work instead of asking "want me to," point time estimates at whoever executes the steps. Same principle as 5: the constraint wins, the shape stays.

## Pre-send check

Before sending, delete:

1. The first sentence if it announces what you are about to do.
2. The last sentence if it asks "anything else?" or recaps what just happened.
3. Any "by the way" sidebar.
4. Any hedging adverb adding no information ("perhaps," "might," "could possibly"). Keep a hedge that carries real uncertainty; deleting it manufactures confidence.
5. Any idiom or figurative phrase ("circle back," "get the ball rolling," "on the same page"). Replace with the literal action.

Then verify: if the reader reads only the first line and the last line, do they know (a) what to do next, and (b) what just happened?

If yes, send.

**What it does:** makes `entire trail list` work with no repo checked out by adding an account-scoped `/me/trails` endpoint.

- home-cell only (no cross-cell fan-out, matches all `/me/*`)
- out of scope: creating a trail outside a repo; the CLI↔API contract drift (deferred to the handoff note)

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# Account-scoped trail listing (`/me/trails`)

Date: 2026-07-28
Repos touched: `entire-api` (new endpoint), `cli` (wiring)

## Problem

`entire trail list` (and the other trail commands) only work from inside a
checked-out repo with a supported `origin` remote. `resolveTrailRepoOrRemote`
resolves a single `forge/owner/repo` triple from `origin` (or the `--repo`
flag) and calls the per-repo endpoint `GET /api/v1/trails/{host}/{owner}/{repo}`
(`cli` `trail_cmd.go:451`, `1974`). With no origin there is no default triple,
so the command errors.

Requiring a checked-out repo just to *list* trails is friction: a user should
be able to see the trails they have access to across all their repos from
anywhere.

## Goals

- `entire trail list` works with no repo checked out, listing trails across all
  repos the caller is a member of.
- Optionally narrow that account-wide list to a subset of repos.
- Reuse the established account-scoped (`/me/*`) and cross-repo (`/cache/prs`)
  server patterns and the home-cell client on the CLI side.

## Non-goals

- Creating a trail from outside a repo (branch+repo bound; tracked separately).
- Cross-jurisdiction aggregation. `/me/trails` is home-cell-only, matching all
  other `/me/*` endpoints; client-side federation is a later follow-up.
- Reconciling the pre-existing repo-scoped list contract drift (tracked in a
  separate local handoff note, not in this spec).

## Server: `/me/trails` endpoint (entire-api)

### Architecture — a `/cache/prs`, not a `/me/activity`

Trails are **repo-store** data (`repo_trails`, keyed by `repo_id`, each row
carrying `author_account_id`) — they are *not* in the per-user `my_activity`
spine. So the endpoint is shaped like `internal/httpapi/cache_prs.go`
(`registerCachePRs`), a cross-repo "your X across your repos" read that needs
only `repoDeps`:

1. `requireAuth` only, no per-repo gate (`router.go:471`).
2. Resolve caller: `id(ctx)` → `auth.FromContext(ctx).AccountID`
   (`experimental_me.go:257`).
3. Enumerate the caller's repos with `memberRepoSet(ctx, deps.Reader)` —
   SpiceDB `repo/list`: direct grants + project membership, **excludes** the
   `public_viewer` wildcard (`perreq.go:53`). Same set `/repos` and
   `/cache/prs` use.
4. If a `repo` filter is present, resolve each `forge/owner/repo` →
   `repo_id` via `RepoIDByFullName` (`store/repo_aggregates.go:559`) and
   **intersect** with the member set. The filter can only narrow, never widen,
   what the caller may see.
5. Query the repo store with the resolved id set (new method, below).
6. Label each row with `repo_full_name` + `is_private` via `repoDisplay` /
   `repoMetaMap` (`me.go:551`, `457`).

### Access model

Default set = **membership** (`repo/list`). Chosen over the accessible/pull set
so the personal list does not pull in every public repo the caller can read.
The `repo` filter still intersects with this set, so access is always
authoritative.

### Wire contract (defined fresh for this endpoint)

Request `GET /api/v1/me/trails`:

| param    | type            | notes                                                             |
|----------|-----------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `status` | comma-list enum | optional; omitted = all statuses                                  |
| `author` | string          | optional; `me` → `author_account_id = caller`. (Arbitrary login not supported in v1 — account-wide has no gh-CLI login lookup.) |
| `repo`   | repeatable / comma-list | optional; each `forge/owner/repo`, intersected with member set |
| `limit`  | int             | clamped (default 200, max TBD in plan)                            |

Response body:

```jsonc
{
  "items": [
    { /* existing TrailListItem fields */
      "repoFullName": "acme/app",
      "isPrivate": true
    }
  ],
  "total": 42
}
```

`items[]` = the existing `TrailListItem` (`trails_types.go:25`) plus
`repoFullName` and `isPrivate`. `total` = full match count for the filters.
No keyset cursor in v1 (limit-capped, matching the `/me/sessions` limit
convention). Sort `updated_at DESC, id DESC`.

### Implementation shape

- **New file** `internal/httpapi/me_trails.go`: `func registerMeTrails(api
  huma.API, deps *RepoActivityDeps)`; input/output structs
  (`MeTrailsInput` / `MeTrailsOutput`), or add the types alongside
  `MeSessionsOutput` in `me_types.go`. Register under the `me` Huma tag.
- **Register** in `internal/httpapi/router.go` `NewActivityAPIRouter`, next to
  `registerMe(...)` / `registerMeSessions(...)` (`router.go:414`).
- **New store method** in `internal/store/trails.go`, alongside
  `ListTrailsByRepo` (`trails.go:67`):
  `TrailsForRepos(ctx, repoIDs [][]byte, filters) ([]TrailListRow, error)` —
  `SELECT ... FROM repo_trails WHERE repo_id = ANY($1) [AND status = ANY(...)]
  [AND author_account_id = $caller] ORDER BY updated_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT $n`,
  plus a count for `total`.
- **Reuse, do not re-implement**: `requireAuth`, `id(ctx)`, `memberRepoSet`,
  `teamOp` (`repos.go:26`), `repoDisplay`/`repoMetaMap`, `isoTime`,
  `resolveAuthorLogins` (`trails.go:265`) for author id→login display.

## CLI wiring (cli)

### Routing rule for `entire trail list`

- **exactly one repo** (`--repo X`, or resolvable `origin`, and no `--all`) →
  repo-scoped endpoint, unchanged. Kept deliberately: the repo-scoped path hits
  the repo's *own* cell, so it is cross-cell safe.
- **zero repos** (no origin / not in a repo), or `--all`, or **multiple repos**
  → account-wide `GET /api/v1/me/trails`, with any repo values passed as the
  `repo` filter.
- Today's hard error on "no resolvable origin" becomes the auto-fallback
  trigger into the account-wide path.

### Client

Account-wide requests use `runAuthenticatedActivityAPI`
(`entireapi_client.go:34`) — the home-cell `auth.NewEntireAPICellClient` with a
data-API fallback — **not** the repo-scoped `runAuthenticatedTrailAPI`
(`trail_context_cache.go:480`) that today's list uses. This is the same client
`/me/activity` and `/me/sessions` use.

### Flags & display

- `--all` (new): force account-wide even inside a repo.
- `--repo`: single value keeps repo-scoped routing (unchanged). Multiple values
  (comma-list or repeatable) route account-wide as a filter. Flag mechanics —
  `--repo` is currently a single persistent `StringVar` on the whole `trail`
  tree (`trail_cmd.go:77`) used by `show`/`checkout` as a single target; the
  plan must pick between accepting a comma-list on the existing flag (with
  single-value validation kept for the subcommands that need exactly one) vs. a
  dedicated list flag scoped to `list`.
- `--status`, `--author me`, `--limit`, `--json` all still apply to the
  account-wide path.
- Account-wide human output adds a **repo column** to `printTrailList`
  (`trail_cmd.go:622`); repo-scoped output is unchanged.

## Limitation

Home-cell only: `/me/trails` sees trails for repos placed in the caller's home
cell that they are a member of. No server-side cross-cell fan-out — consistent
with every `/me/*` endpoint. A `repo` filter naming a repo hosted in another
cell returns nothing from `/me/trails`; that single repo is better listed via
the repo-scoped path (which is why single `--repo` stays repo-scoped).

## Testing

- **entire-api**: store-level test for `TrailsForRepos` (id-set filter, status
  filter, author filter, ordering, limit/total). httpapi test for
  `/me/trails`: membership gating (a non-member repo's trails never appear),
  the `repo` filter intersecting with membership (cannot widen access), and
  the response shape incl. `repoFullName`/`isPrivate`. Follow the
  `cache_prs` / `me_sessions` test patterns.
- **cli**: routing tests — one repo vs. zero vs. multiple vs. `--all` picks the
  right endpoint/client; account-wide `--json` output; repo column rendering;
  `--author me` maps to the account filter. Use `execx.NonInteractive` for any
  real-binary spawns.

## Sequencing

1. entire-api: `TrailsForRepos` store method + `/me/trails` handler + tests.
2. cli: routing + flags + display + tests, targeting the new contract.

The CLI account-wide path depends on the entire-api endpoint existing, so land
the server side first (or behind the same review).

# Account-scoped trail listing (`/me/trails`)

Date: 2026-07-28
Repos touched: `entire-api` (new endpoint), `cli` (wiring)

## Problem

`entire trail list` (and the other trail commands) only work from inside a
checked-out repo with a supported `origin` remote. `resolveTrailRepoOrRemote`
resolves a single `forge/owner/repo` triple from `origin` (or the `--repo`
flag) and calls the per-repo endpoint `GET /api/v1/trails/{host}/{owner}/{repo}`
(`cli` `trail_cmd.go:451`, `1974`). With no origin there is no default triple,
so the command errors.

Requiring a checked-out repo just to *list* trails is friction: a user should
be able to see the trails they have access to across all their repos from
anywhere.

## Goals

- `entire trail list` works with no repo checked out, listing trails across all
  repos the caller is a member of.
- Optionally narrow that account-wide list to a subset of repos.
- `entire trail show <trail>` works from anywhere by resolving the trail's repo
  from the account index.
- **No change to in-repo behavior.** `entire trail list` / `trail show` inside a
  repo with a resolvable `origin` (and no `--all`) hit the exact same
  repo-scoped endpoint, client, and output as today.
- Reuse the established account-scoped (`/me/*`) and cross-repo (`/cache/prs`)
  server patterns and the home-cell client on the CLI side.

## Non-goals

- Repo-less support for API-write commands (`comment`, `approve`,
  `request-changes`, `update`, `delete`, `watch`). These are server calls and
  *could* work repo-less on top of the same resolve-from-account step, but are
  out of scope this pass — follow-up.
- Repo-less support for local-clone commands (`checkout`, `resume`, `create`).
  These inherently need a working tree/branch; not applicable.
- Cross-jurisdiction aggregation. `/me/trails` is home-cell-only, matching all
  other `/me/*` endpoints; client-side federation is a later follow-up.
- Reconciling the pre-existing repo-scoped list contract drift (tracked in a
  separate local handoff note, not in this spec).

## Server: `/me/trails` endpoint (entire-api)

### Architecture — a `/cache/prs`, not a `/me/activity`

Trails are **repo-store** data (`repo_trails`, keyed by `repo_id`, each row
carrying `author_account_id`) — they are *not* in the per-user `my_activity`
spine. So the endpoint is shaped like `internal/httpapi/cache_prs.go`
(`registerCachePRs`), a cross-repo "your X across your repos" read that needs
only `repoDeps`:

1. `requireAuth` only, no per-repo gate (`router.go:471`).
2. Resolve caller: `id(ctx)` → `auth.FromContext(ctx).AccountID`
   (`experimental_me.go:257`).
3. Enumerate the caller's repos with `memberRepoSet(ctx, deps.Reader)` —
   SpiceDB `repo/list`: direct grants + project membership, **excludes** the
   `public_viewer` wildcard (`perreq.go:53`). Same set `/repos` and
   `/cache/prs` use.
4. If a `repo` filter is present, resolve each `forge/owner/repo` →
   `repo_id` via `RepoIDByFullName` (`store/repo_aggregates.go:559`) and
   **intersect** with the member set. The filter can only narrow, never widen,
   what the caller may see.
5. Query the repo store with the resolved id set (new method, below).
6. Label each row with `repo_full_name` + `is_private` via `repoDisplay` /
   `repoMetaMap` (`me.go:551`, `457`).

### Access model

Default set = **membership** (`repo/list`). Chosen over the accessible/pull set
so the personal list does not pull in every public repo the caller can read.
The `repo` filter still intersects with this set, so access is always
authoritative.

### Wire contract (defined fresh for this endpoint)

Request `GET /api/v1/me/trails`:

| param    | type            | notes                                                             |
|----------|-----------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `status` | comma-list enum | optional; omitted = all statuses                                  |
| `author` | string          | optional; `me` → `author_account_id = caller`. (Arbitrary login not supported in v1 — account-wide has no gh-CLI login lookup.) |
| `repo`   | repeatable / comma-list | optional; each `forge/owner/repo`, intersected with member set |
| `limit`  | int             | clamped (default 200, max TBD in plan)                            |

Response body:

```jsonc
{
  "items": [
    { /* existing TrailListItem fields */
      "repoFullName": "acme/app",
      "isPrivate": true
    }
  ],
  "total": 42
}
```

`items[]` = the existing `TrailListItem` (`trails_types.go:25`) plus
`repoFullName` and `isPrivate`. `total` = full match count for the filters.
No keyset cursor in v1 (limit-capped, matching the `/me/sessions` limit
convention). Sort `updated_at DESC, id DESC`.

### Implementation shape

- **New file** `internal/httpapi/me_trails.go`: `func registerMeTrails(api
  huma.API, deps *RepoActivityDeps)`; input/output structs
  (`MeTrailsInput` / `MeTrailsOutput`), or add the types alongside
  `MeSessionsOutput` in `me_types.go`. Register under the `me` Huma tag.
- **Register** in `internal/httpapi/router.go` `NewActivityAPIRouter`, next to
  `registerMe(...)` / `registerMeSessions(...)` (`router.go:414`).
- **New store method** in `internal/store/trails.go`, alongside
  `ListTrailsByRepo` (`trails.go:67`):
  `TrailsForRepos(ctx, repoIDs [][]byte, filters) ([]TrailListRow, error)` —
  `SELECT ... FROM repo_trails WHERE repo_id = ANY($1) [AND status = ANY(...)]
  [AND author_account_id = $caller] ORDER BY updated_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT $n`,
  plus a count for `total`.
- **Reuse, do not re-implement**: `requireAuth`, `id(ctx)`, `memberRepoSet`,
  `teamOp` (`repos.go:26`), `repoDisplay`/`repoMetaMap`, `isoTime`,
  `resolveAuthorLogins` (`trails.go:265`) for author id→login display.

## CLI wiring (cli)

### Routing rule for `entire trail list`

- **exactly one repo** (`--repo X`, or resolvable `origin`, and no `--all`) →
  repo-scoped endpoint, unchanged. Kept deliberately: the repo-scoped path hits
  the repo's *own* cell, so it is cross-cell safe.
- **zero repos** (no origin / not in a repo), or `--all`, or **multiple repos**
  → account-wide `GET /api/v1/me/trails`, with any repo values passed as the
  `repo` filter.
- Today's hard error on "no resolvable origin" becomes the auto-fallback
  trigger into the account-wide path.

### Client

Account-wide requests use `runAuthenticatedActivityAPI`
(`entireapi_client.go:34`) — the home-cell `auth.NewEntireAPICellClient` with a
data-API fallback — **not** the repo-scoped `runAuthenticatedTrailAPI`
(`trail_context_cache.go:480`) that today's list uses. This is the same client
`/me/activity` and `/me/sessions` use.

### Flags & display

- `--all` (new): force account-wide even inside a repo.
- `--repo`: single value keeps repo-scoped routing (unchanged). Multiple values
  (comma-list or repeatable) route account-wide as a filter. Flag mechanics —
  `--repo` is currently a single persistent `StringVar` on the whole `trail`
  tree (`trail_cmd.go:77`) used by `show`/`checkout` as a single target; the
  plan must pick between accepting a comma-list on the existing flag (with
  single-value validation kept for the subcommands that need exactly one) vs. a
  dedicated list flag scoped to `list`.
- `--status`, `--author me`, `--limit`, `--json` all still apply to the
  account-wide path.
- Account-wide human output adds a **repo column** to `printTrailList`
  (`trail_cmd.go:622`); repo-scoped output is unchanged.

## Limitation

Home-cell only: `/me/trails` sees trails for repos placed in the caller's home
cell that they are a member of. No server-side cross-cell fan-out — consistent
with every `/me/*` endpoint. A `repo` filter naming a repo hosted in another
cell returns nothing from `/me/trails`; that single repo is better listed via
the repo-scoped path (which is why single `--repo` stays repo-scoped).

## Testing

- **entire-api**: store-level test for `TrailsForRepos` (id-set filter, status
  filter, author filter, ordering, limit/total). httpapi test for
  `/me/trails`: membership gating (a non-member repo's trails never appear),
  the `repo` filter intersecting with membership (cannot widen access), and
  the response shape incl. `repoFullName`/`isPrivate`. Follow the
  `cache_prs` / `me_sessions` test patterns.
- **cli**: routing tests — one repo vs. zero vs. multiple vs. `--all` picks the
  right endpoint/client; account-wide `--json` output; repo column rendering;
  `--author me` maps to the account filter. Use `execx.NonInteractive` for any
  real-binary spawns.

## Sequencing

1. entire-api: `TrailsForRepos` store method + `/me/trails` handler + tests.
2. cli: routing + flags + display + tests, targeting the new contract.

The CLI account-wide path depends on the entire-api endpoint existing, so land
the server side first (or behind the same review).

Base directory for this skill: /Users/ninawork/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.2.0/skills/writing-plans

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## No Placeholders

Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** — never write them:
- "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
- "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
- "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
- "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code — the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
- Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
- References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags — any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan, offer execution choice:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Two execution options:**

**1. Subagent-Driven (recommended)** - I dispatch a fresh subagent per task, review between tasks, fast iteration

**2. Inline Execution** - Execute tasks in this session using executing-plans, batch execution with checkpoints

**Which approach?"**

**If Subagent-Driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

**If Inline Execution chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review

func runTrailListAllWithClient(ctx context.Context, w io.Writer, client *api.Client, opts trailListOptions, statusFilters []trail.Status) error {
	authorFilter := opts.Author
	currentUserLogin := ""
	if authorFilter == trailListAuthorMe {
		login, err := fetchCurrentUserLogin(ctx, execRunner{})
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		currentUserLogin = login
		authorFilter = login
	}

	forge, owner, repo, err := resolveTrailRepoOrRemote(ctx, opts.Repo)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	// Filtering, sorting (updated_at desc), and truncation all happen
	// server-side; the response carries the total match count so a capped
	// page never reads as the total number of matches.
	resp, err := client.Get(ctx, trailsBasePath(forge, owner, repo)+trailListQuery(statusFilters, authorFilter, opts.Limit))
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("failed to list trails: %w", err)
	}
	defer resp.Body.Close()
	if err := checkTrailResponse(resp); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	var listResp api.TrailListResponse
	if err := api.DecodeJSON(resp, &listResp); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("failed to decode trail list: %w", err)
	}

	// Convert to metadata for display, attaching the browser URL (server-provided
	// when present, locally constructed as a fallback for older servers).
	trails := make([]*trail.Metadata, 0, len(listResp.Trails))
	for i := range listResp.Trails {
		m := listResp.Trails[i].ToMetadata()
		m.URL = trailDisplayURL(listResp.Trails[i], forge, owner, repo)
		trails = append(trails, m)
	}

	totalMatched := listResp.Total
	if totalMatched < len(trails) {
		// Older servers don't report a total; fall back to the page size.
		totalMatched = len(trails)
	}

	if opts.JSON {
		enc := json.NewEncoder(w)
		enc.SetIndent("", "  ")
		if err := enc.Encode(trails); err != nil {
			return fmt.Errorf("failed to encode JSON: %w", err)
		}
		return nil
	}

	if len(trails) == 0 {
		printTrailListEmpty(w, authorFilter, statusFilters)
		return nil
	}

	printTrailList(w, trails, trailListDisplayOptions{
		RequestedAuthor: authorFilter,
		CurrentUser:     currentUserLogin,
		StatusFilters:   statusFilters,
		TotalMatched:    totalMatched,
	})

	if opts.Limit > trailListServerMaxLimit && totalMatched > len(trails) {
		fmt.Fprintln(w)
		fmt.Fprintf(w, "Note: --limit %d exceeds the server maximum of %d trails per request.\n", opts.Limit, trailListServerMaxLimit)
	}

	return nil
}

func printTrailListHeader(w io.Writer, opts trailListDisplayOptions, count int) {

	// The noun refers to the full match set, so pluralize by the total when
	// the page is truncated ("1/2 trails", not "1/2 trail").
	nounCount := count

	if opts.RequestedAuthor == "" {

func printTrailRows(w io.Writer, trails []*trail.Metadata, showAuthor, showStatus bool) {
	styles := newStatusStyles(w)
	showPhase := trailListHasPhase(trails)
	showURL := trailListHasURL(trails)

	// The leading two-space indent is folded into the first column so the shared
	// table renderer (columnWidths/writeTableRow) reproduces the list's layout.
	headers := []string{"  NUM", "BRANCH", "TITLE"}
	if showStatus {
		headers = append(headers, "STATUS")
	}
	if showPhase {
		headers = append(headers, "PHASE")
	}
	if showAuthor {
		headers = append(headers, "AUTHOR")
	}
	headers = append(headers, "UPDATED")
	if showURL {
		headers = append(headers, "URL")
	}

	rows := make([][]string, len(trails))
	for i, t := range trails {
		number := "-"
		if t.Number > 0 {
			number = strconv.Itoa(t.Number)
		}
		title := truncateOneLine(t.Title, 60)
		if title == "" {
			title = "(untitled)"
		}
		fields := []string{"  " + number, t.Branch, title}
		// Cells are pre-colored here; columnWidths/writeTableRow measure width
		// with lipgloss.Width (ANSI-agnostic), so color never shifts columns.
		if showStatus {
			status := trailStatusDisplay(t.Status)
			if style, ok := trailStatusColor(styles, t.Status); ok {
				status = styles.render(style, status)
			}
			fields = append(fields, status)
		}
		if showPhase {
			phase := trailPhaseDisplay(t.Phase)
			if styles.colorEnabled && phase != "-" {
				phase = styles.render(styles.yellow, phase)
			}
			fields = append(fields, phase)
		}
		if showAuthor {
			author := t.AuthorLogin()
			if styles.colorEnabled && author != "" {
				author = styles.render(styles.cyan, author)
			}
			fields = append(fields, author)
		}
		fields = append(fields, timeAgo(t.UpdatedAt))
		if showURL {
			fields = append(fields, t.URL)
		}
		rows[i] = fields
	}

	widths := columnWidths(headers, rows)
	var b strings.Builder
	// Header row is yellow; data cells are already pre-colored, so they pass
	// through a disabled style. tblSt only supplies the color-enabled gate for
	// the header style.
	tblSt := newTableStyles(w)
	headerStyle := func(int) lipgloss.Style { return styles.yellow }
	plain := func(int) lipgloss.Style { return lipgloss.Style{} }
	writeTableRow(&b, headers, widths, headerStyle, tblSt)
	for _, r := range rows {
		writeTableRow(&b, r, widths, plain, tableStyles{})
	}
	fmt.Fprint(w, b.String())
}
